title: Attention Sink Forges Native MoE in Attention Layers: Sink-Aware Training to Address Head Collapse
claim: Different attention variants route gating differently: implicit via the softmax sink or explicit via a learned gate, revealing a shared mixture-of-experts structure.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, parallel block diagrams with dashed green highlight boxes
description: Three side-by-side block diagrams on gray rounded backgrounds compare attention variants: Vanilla Attention, Sink Attention and Gated Attention. Each panel has a title and model logos with names (Qwen, LLaMA, GPT-OSS, DeepSeek). Data flows bottom to top through three Linear layers producing q, k and v, then MatMul, Softmax, a second MatMul and a final multiply-circle gate. Vanilla and Sink panels use red 'Implicit Gating' labels and dashed green boxes around the softmax. They also show sigma-of-lse formulas. Sink Attention adds a Sink term to the softmax denominator, shown in red. Gated Attention uses a red 'Explicit Gating' branch with an extra Linear layer and sigma(xW) gate. A purple 'No attention sink' label sits above the Gated panel. Pink, beige, blue and green boxes distinguish the module types.
caption: Vanilla Attention used in most open-source models. Sink Attention used in GPT-OSS with a learnable bias sink added to the softmax denominator. Gated Attention used in Qwen3-Next with a head-wise gating factor computed via sigmoid activation.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often assign disproportionate attention to the first token, a phenomenon known as the attention sink. Several recent approaches aim to address this issue, including Sink Attention in GPT-OSS and Gated Attention in Qwen3-Next. However, a comprehensive analysis of the relationship among these attention mechanisms is lacking. In this work, we provide both theoretical and empirical evidence demonstrating that the sink in Vanilla Attention and Sink Attention naturally construct a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism within attention layers. This insight explains the head collapse phenomenon observed in prior work, where only a fixed subset of attention heads contributes to generation. To mitigate head collapse, we propose a sink-aware training algorithm with an auxiliary load balancing loss designed for attention layers. Extensive experiments show that our method achieves effective head load balancing and improves model performance across Vanilla Attention, Sink Attention, and Gated Attention. We hope this study offers a new perspective on attention mechanisms and encourages further exploration of the inherent MoE structure within attention layers.
